text: Skim foam or fat off the top of a boiling liquid.
Clean out and replace an aquarium or terrarium filter.

Kids: bedtime routine (bath-water temperature check, pajamas, story, night light, checking on a sleeping child), bottle and formula prep, sterilizing, supervised play (catch, hide-and-seek, card and board games), reading aloud.

section: Emergency response (must-have). Detection and alerting are covered well, but active response is thin.
text: Respond: shut off the main water, a fixture valve, or gas; use a fire extinguisher; evacuate people and pets; call emergency services and relay the address and symptoms; unlock the door and guide responders; fetch the AED and first-aid kit; run a power-outage routine (flashlights, unplug sensitive electronics, protect the fridge and freezer); shelter during severe weather; know where the breaker panel and shutoffs are.

section: Reaching, climbing, and fixing. Tool handling stops at basic hand tools, and there's no height access.
text: Repairs: paint walls and touch up scuffs, caulk a tub or sink, patch small holes, sand, regrout, pressure-wash, seal a deck.

text: Small plumbing and fixes: unclog sinks and shower drains, fix a running toilet, reset a garbage disposal, clear a printer jam, bleed a radiator.
Clean up broken glass and ceramic, spilled flour, sugar, or oil, vomit, urine, and pet accidents.
Maintain other household robots: empty the robot vacuum, clean its brushes, refill the mop tank, rescue it when stuck, clear cords and socks before it runs.

Away mode. Your departure routine covers daily exits. Add a vacation or house-sitting mode: arm the alarm, set lights on timers, bring in mail and packages, water plants, check for leaks and pests, run taps, check the freezer after an outage, care for pets, send status photos.

Pets beyond feeding and walking. Give owner-directed medication, bathe and dry a dog, check for ticks and fleas, open and close crates, keep pets' meals separate, calm a pet during storms or fireworks. Aquarium water changes, filter, and glass, small-animal cages, and backyard chickens (eggs, coop, water) are also missing.
“Deal with this mess.” It has to inspect the situation and create its own cleanup plan.
“Do the important stuff first.” Requires ranking chores by urgency and impact.
“Check the house before we leave.” It has to inspect locks, windows, appliances, pets, lights, faucets, garage doors, and other household-specific concerns.
“Carry this without tipping it.” Requires estimating center of mass and liquid movement.
“Clean the spots people usually miss.” Requires knowledge of common cleaning failures.
“Find where that smell is coming from.” Requires active investigation across rooms and possible causes.
“There’s a weird noise somewhere.” Requires localization, appliance knowledge, and anomaly detection.
“Make sure nothing looks wrong.” General anomaly detection across an open world.
“Untangle the garden hose.” Larger-scale flexible-object planning.
“Water anything that needs water.” Requires plant identification and soil/moisture judgment.
“Take care of the plants while I’m gone.” Different plants may need different schedules and amounts.
“Open this carbonated drink without it exploding.” Requires force control, auditory/tactile feedback to detect pressure release, and pacing.
“Arrange these flowers so they look nice.” Requires aesthetic planning, understanding balance, height, and color distribution.
“Run the house while we’re away for a week.” Requires long-horizon autonomy, contingency handling, and knowing when to escalate.
“Learn the house.” Requires mapping rooms, objects, owners, no-go zones, shutoff locations, and the emergency plan, including in a home that isn’t yours.
“Get ready for the storm / the plumber / the newborn.” Requires building an event-specific prep list from context.
